about: The fish genera's own presentation and ID marks, for the circle-1 genera the IMR fish presentation gives no cues for (Pierre, 2026-11-08: each genus needs a short presentation and its ID cues, sourced, rules C2, C3, C6, before the genera open to more players). Our own words, never copied, written from public sources: src, each {t, u}, t starting with the source's short name before its first comma. families: the families done (every circle-1 genus of these without IMR cues is in genera with marks, or in none with its reason). genera, by genus name: plain, [one or two sentences on what the genus looks like and how it lives, its refs]; marks, 1 to 3 [visible feature that tells it from the other genera of its family, its refs], a ref being [src key, where in it (key couplet or species account, page)]. Only features seen on a photo: never a fin-ray, spine or scale count, a tooth or a feature inside the mouth; a species named is one of the genus's game species (rule C6). none: a genus left without marks and why (no visible feature in the sources read): never a mark guessed. A genus with IMR cues is never here: the IMR cues stay apart (rule C1). tools/build_fish.py add_families puts plain, marks, msrc and mby on fish.json genera; app.js fishGenera shows them on the genus card, learn.js genMarks on the sheet the genus opens.

fao-lab.t: FAO species guide, Labridae (Westneat 2001), key to the genera

plain: Bold wrasses of shallow coral and rocky reefs; some, such as T. amblycephalum, gather above the reef to feed on plankton.
marks: Short, blunt snout, never drawn out into a tube (Gomphosus)

plain: Wrasses whose long, thin jaws pick small animals out of cracks in coral and rock, from 1 to 15 m.
marks: Snout drawn out into a long, thin tube made by both jaws

plain: Small, slender wrasses; L. dimidiatus keeps cleaning stations where other fishes come to have their parasites picked off, even inside the mouth and gills.
marks: Lower lip split in two by a deep notch

plain: Wrasses of shallow lagoon reefs rich in coral, where they eat coral polyps, above all of staghorn Acropora.
marks: Lips that close into a short tube
Body deeper than Labroides, the lower lip not split

plain: Small wrasses, about 10 cm, of sheltered lagoons rich in coral: adults eat coral polyps, juveniles clean other fishes.
marks: Lips that close into a short tube

plain: Small wrasses of rich coral reefs, alone or in small groups; adults eat coral polyps and may also clean other fishes.
marks: Lips that close into a short tube
Rounded snout profile in adults (Diproctacanthus: straight)

plain: Deep-bodied wrasses of coral reefs and the sand or seagrass nearby; they feed mostly on hard-shelled animals such as molluscs and crustaceans.
marks: Body as deep as the head is long, or deeper
Jaws end level at the front
Often vertical bars, or pale spots on a dark body

plain: Slimmer cousins of Cheilinus that hunt small fishes, shrimps and other crustaceans on coral reefs.
marks: Body less deep than the head is long
Lower jaw juts out beyond the upper
Often a stripe along the body, or a black spot at the front of the dorsal fin

plain: Wrasses whose jaws can shoot far forward, as a long tube, to snap up prey.
marks: Mouth closed, the long lower jaw reaches back under the head to the gill cover

plain: Small, shy wrasses that keep among coral branches on seaward reefs and eat small crustaceans.
marks: Dorsal and anal fins low (Paracheilinus: tall, often with filaments)

plain: Small wrasses, about 8 cm, that school above coral or rubble at the foot of steep outer reef slopes; males are larger and more colourful than females.
marks: Dorsal and anal fins tall and colourful, often with trailing filaments

plain: Wrasses of the sand and rubble around reefs that turn over rocks to find the animals beneath; the juveniles look like drifting seaweed.
marks: Head sloping gently to the snout (Iniistius: almost vertical)
Dark bands radiating from the eye across a pale head
Dark body with a white spot on each scale

plain: Razorfishes of open sand: they hover just above the bottom and dive head first into the sand when danger comes.
marks: Blunt head, dropping almost vertically to the snout

plain: Large wrasses, up to about 50 cm, of coral reefs and reef flats; H. melapterus takes in mouthfuls of sand, sorts out the small animals and blows the sand out.
marks: Very thick, fleshy lips, the upper one jutting beyond the lower
Adults: pink and blue-green bands on the head

plain: Small, secretive wrasses that hide among dense weed, from shallow reefs with algae to deeper soft bottoms.
marks: Adults brown to dark red with blotches

plain: Wrasses of mixed coral, rubble and sand on seaward reefs; males and females are often coloured very differently.
marks: In most species a coloured spot or bar on each scale

plain: Small wrasses with a deep, flattened body and a striking pattern of spots or bands.
marks: Bright bands on head and body, or bright blotches, or a spot on each scale

plain: A large genus of mostly small wrasses of coral reefs, rocky shores and the sand nearby.
marks: Body less deep than Macropharyngodon, the dorsal fin starting further back

plain: Small wrasses that swim fast in small groups over shallow reefs and reef flats, beating their pectoral fins.
marks: Pectoral fins set high, just behind the gill cover

plain: Long, slim wrasses, up to about 50 cm, of shallow back reefs and weedy areas; they eat crustaceans and small fishes.
Long-bodied wrasses of coral reefs and rocky bottoms that hunt small fishes and crustaceans.
marks: Long snout with fleshy lips (Coris: short snout)

plain: Wrasses of coral reefs and lagoons that eat hard-shelled prey; the young can look nothing like the adults, as in C. gaimard.
Small wrasses, C. lubbocki about 7 cm, that feed on plankton just above coral rubble and small branching corals on outer reefs.
marks: Males often brilliant red, purple or blue

plain: Solitary wrasses of rock and coral reefs, to about 60 m, that scrape small animals off the bottom; the juveniles pick parasites from other fishes.
marks: Grey to purplish, with a reddish spot on each scale

plain: Wrasses of coral reefs; B. axillaris eats molluscs and crustaceans, and its young live in coral caves and sometimes clean other fishes.
Solitary wrasses of shallow coral reefs and seagrass beds that eat crustaceans, molluscs and sea urchins.

none.Bodianus: the FAO key (couplets 2, 4, 5) sets it apart by spine, ray and scale counts and the scales of the cheek and fins only: nothing seen on a photo
none.Choerodon: the FAO key (couplets 2, 4) sets it apart by spine counts, canine teeth and small cheek scales only: nothing seen on a photo
none.Cymolutes: the FAO key (couplet 14) sets it apart by anal spines and scale counts only: nothing seen on a photo
none.Novaculoides: the FAO key (2001) puts its species in Novaculichthys, whose colour there fits N. taeniourus only: no source of its own read
none.Wetmorella: the FAO key (couplet 10) sets it apart by the scales of the cheek and gill cover only: nothing seen on a photo
